title: Efficient biological carbon export to the mesopelagic ocean induced by submesoscale fronts

paper_content.abstract: Oceanic submesoscale processes are ubiquitous in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG), where the biological carbon pump is generally ineffective. Due to difficulties in collecting continuous observations, however, it remains uncertain whether episodic submesoscale processes can drive significant changes in particulate organic carbon (POC) export into the mesopelagic ocean. Here we present observations from high-frequency Biogeochemical-Argo floats in the NPSG, which captured the enhanced POC export fluxes during the intensifying stages of a submesoscale front and a cyclonic eddy compared to their other life stages. A higher percentage of POC export flux was found to be transferred to the base of mesopelagic layer at the front compared to that at the intensifying eddy and the mean of previous studies (37% vs. ~10%), suggesting that the POC export efficiency was significantly strengthened by submesoscale dynamics. Such findings highlight the importance of submesoscale fronts for carbon export and sequestration in subtropical gyres.
paper_content.introduction:
Biological pumping of particulate organic carbon (POC), one of the primary mechanisms that draws atmospheric CO2 to the deep sea, has been reported to be ineffective within oligotrophic gyres, such as the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG)1–3. In these regions, weak vertical nutrient supply limits biological productivity4 and consequently reduces carbon export5,6. Furthermore, the downward POC flux attenuates rapidly in the mesopelagic layer due to the dominance of small-size sinking particles7, considerable fragmentation8, and relatively fast remineralization compared to that at high latitudes9–11.

Subtropical gyres have abundant mesoscale eddies characterized by small Rossby numbers (Ro) and large Richardson numbers (Ri), as well as submesoscale fronts characterized by O(1) Ro and Ri12–16. Mesoscale eddies and submesoscale fronts can impact biological pumps in various ways16–24. Generally, mesoscale eddies experience different life stages, such as the intensifying, mature, and decaying stages. The stage during eddy formation and intensification is typically associated with upward isopycnal displacement in cyclonic eddies (CEs) and downward displacement in anticyclonic eddies (ACEs). The upward isopycnal displacement during a CE intensifying stage can increase nutrient supply and primary production25–28, enhancing POC sinking in subtropical gyres (referred to as the biological gravitational pump)29–31. Due to the increase in the lateral buoyancy gradient32, intensifying submesoscale fronts are often accompanied by vertical velocities as high as 10–100 m d−1, which is an order of magnitude greater than the vertical velocities induced by mesoscale eddies14,15. These vertical motions can inject high quantities of POC produced in the euphotic zone into the mesopelagic layer (referred to as subduction pump)17,19,22,24, resulting in carbon sequestration17,19,20,23. The vertical motions induced by submesoscale fronts may also drive the vertical nutrient supply and stimulate the growth of large phytoplankton communities32–36; these large phytoplankton may sink fast and affect the carbon export efficiency by creating particles with fast sinking velocities through food web dynamics16,36,37. At the global scale, submesoscale fronts have the potential to contribute to POC export38,39, which would help to reconcile the imbalance between the upper layer carbon supply and deep ocean carbon consumption9,17,40.

Prior studies have captured anomalous features of elevated POC at depth, which are interpreted as evidence of the subduction pump19,22,23. Despite their potential importance in shaping POC export, direct observations of the downward POC flux and its attenuation in response to submesoscale fronts are scarce17,19–21,23,41. This is largely attributable to their relatively small spatiotemporal scales and the difficulty in obtaining subsurface observations, as well as the possible decoupling between physical and biogeochemical processes at the front41. Mesoscale features have been suggested to be able to change the strength of oceanic carbon export locally29–31,42,43, whereas the effects of submesoscale features are still unclear. Using high-resolution simulations, Omand et al.19 showed that the subduction pump contributes up to 50% of the spring POC flux in the North Atlantic and Southern Ocean. However, Llort et al.23 showed that the contribution ranged between 1% in spring and 14–19% in summer in the Southern Ocean. By using a model covering a subpolar and a subtropical gyre, Resplandy et al.18 suggested that the subduction pump contributes less than 5% to the annual carbon export due to the strong compensation between upward and downward fluxes at the basin scale. Given the large uncertainty among the estimations from different studies, more high-resolution field observations are required.

There are challenges when estimating the POC export flux associated with episodic submesoscale features by either sediment traps or radioactive pairs (mainly the 234Th-238U pair). Biogeochemical-Argo (BGC-Argo) floats can fill observational gaps over small spatial and temporal scales20,23,28,44,45. By tracking the particle accumulation rates in the water column over sustained periods, BGC-Argo data have been used to estimate the downward POC flux8,45–48. BGC-Argo data include variables that may change in both space and time, especially when sampled near mesoscale and submesoscale features. Thus, careful analysis is required to reasonably delineate the temporal rates and/or the spatial variability of measured variables. The BGC-Argo has been used to identify elevated POC in the mesopelagic layer and estimate the carbon flux associated with submesoscale features20,23. However, the transfer efficiency of POC export associated with submesoscale features has rarely been investigated.

In this study, we show the capability of using BGC-Argo floats to estimate the efficiency of POC export in response to submesoscale fronts and eddies. We deployed two high-frequency sampling floats that profiled twice a day in the western NPSG. These two floats captured the intensifying stages of a mesoscale eddy and a submesoscale front, which were used to estimate vertically resolved POC export fluxes and transfer efficiencies. Further data synthesis extrapolating the results to the entire subtropical gyre revealed the important role that submesoscale fronts may play in strengthening the biological POC pump in the mesopelagic ocean.
paper_content.results:
Site characterization and tracer distributions
Two BGC-Argo floats (WMO numbers 2902753 and 2902756; Fig. 1a, Table S1 and Text S1) were deployed in two cyclonic eddies (identified as CE1 and CE2; Fig. 1a, Table S2 and Text S2) to collect temperature, salinity, nitrate, chlorophyll-a (Chl), dissolved oxygen (DO), particulate backscattering coefficients at 700 nm (bbp(700)) and photosynthetically available radiation (PAR). From 30 March to 20 April 2019, float 2902753 moved gradually from the CE1 core to the CE1 edge with the relative position r/R (r and R were the distance of the float to the eddy center and the eddy radius, respectively) increasing from ~0 to 2 (Fig. 1b and Fig. 2a). During this time, the sea level anomaly (SLA) at the float position increased gradually from −0.1 m to 0.1 m, reflecting the SLA change from the CE1 center to its periphery (Fig. 1b). From 21 April to 3 May 2019, this float moved along one side of a submesoscale front and experienced the intensifying and decaying stages of the front (Fig. 1b). Float 2902756 was deployed and trapped in the core region of CE2 and experienced the intensifying and mature stages of the eddy until 22 April 2019 (Figs. 1c and 2b).

The euphotic depth (ZEu) was on average ~159 m within CE1 and changed slightly along the radial direction (Fig. S1). The floats may have captured the spatial variability of tracers for CE1 as the location of the floats changed from inside to outside the eddy. The satellite-derived sea surface Chl was averaged over the float sampling period and then interpolated onto the relative locations of the float in CE1 to compare with that measured by the float. The float-measured Chl was in agreement with that derived from satellites in the radial direction (Fig. S2a), with a correlation of 0.39 (p=0.01). In contrast, the temporal evolution of satellite-derived Chl averaged inside CE1 was different from that of float-measured Chl (Fig. S2b), as indicated by a low correlation (R=−0.18, p=0.24). Therefore, the float-measured tracers during this period can be used to represent the spatial variability of CE1 along the radial direction. The radial POC distributions of CE1 were constructed from BGC-Argo measurements (Fig. 3). From the center to the edge, the POC distributions in CE1 decreased at the subsurface chlorophyll maximum depth (ZSCM; on average 117.0 ± 9.9 m; Fig. S1) and increased at 200 m depth. The radial POC distributions at 400 m and 600 m changed slightly compared with those at 200 m. As the float moved to the edge of CE1, the temperature displayed an increasing trend, while nitrate, Chl and POC showed a decreasing trend (Fig. S3 and Table S3). This result suggested that nutrients in the euphotic zone were enhanced by the uplift of isotherms within this cyclonic eddy28, leading to higher POC concentrations in the CE1 center than at its edge (Fig. 3). The POC at 200 m reached its peaks at the edge of r/R=~1 and 1.3, which was likely due to subduction of POC from the productive layer by the front17,19,20,23. This observation further supported that the radial distributions of POC measured by the float reflected the spatial variability of the eddy.

POC flux by an intensifying cyclonic eddy (CE2)
We defined the intensifying and mature stages of CE2 based on the temporal change of SLA averaged inside CE2. Data from float 2902756 were then classified into intensifying-stage and mature-stage measurements by comparing the change of SLA near the float with that averaged inside CE2. From 6 April to 14 April 2019, the CE2 intensified with gradually decreasing SLA values (Fig. S4). The SLA near the float also decreased gradually from −0.03 m to -0.09 m until 14 April, almost synchronously with the SLA decrease inside CE2 (Fig. S4). Additionally, the SLA change of the float was positively correlated with the change in temperature and negatively correlated with the changes in NO3−, Chl and POC at the ZSCM (Fig. S5 and Table S3), implying that the float captured the eddy’s intensifying stage. In stages other than the intensifying stage, the correlations between changes in SLA and changes in temperature, NO3−, Chl, and POC at the ZSCM were generally low or even insignificant (Fig. S5). From April 15 to April 22, the SLA near the float and that averaged inside CE2 remained at extremely low values, indicating that the eddy had reached a mature stage. Except for a fluctuation in the relative position (r/R) during the first few days, the float’s r/R value inside CE2 remained approximately 0.7 until 22 April 2019 (Fig. 1c). We thus used the float measurements during 6–14 April to describe the eddy’s intensifying stage and measurements during 15–22 April to describe the eddy’s mature stage.

Since float 2902756 traveled in a quasi-Lagrangian manner inside the eddy during the intensifying and mature eddy stages, we assumed that the variability measured by the float was mostly attributable to temporal changes of the eddy. The POC concentration was first integrated from the base of the mesopelagic layer (900 m) to depth z (integrated POC; noted as P(z) in Eq. (3)), and then the rate at which POC changed over time (denoted as E(z)) was computed by Eq. (4). With multiple sampling profiles, a linear least squared method (slope of the regression line) was used to estimate E(z) during the intensifying (denoted as E_EI(z)) and mature (denoted as E_EM(z)) stages. Negative E_EM(z) values were present at all depths (Fig. 4a, c), which suggested that the POC removal process was dominant for the POC concentration change during the mature stage of the eddy, likely caused by microbial degradation in the mesopelagic layer9,49. Consistent with other observational studies35, the rate of change of POC decreased gradually with depth in the mesopelagic layer. However, there was a significant difference between the E_EI(z) and E_EM(z) profiles (Fig. 4c). The E_EI(z) during the intensifying stage of the eddy was larger than the E_EM(z), and their difference decreased with depth. This suggested a decrease in the rate of change of POC in the mature stage with respect to the intensifying stage, which could be induced by changes in the POC export flux from the top and/or the POC consumption rate in the water column. In addition, the net rate of change of apparent oxygen utilization (AOU) was positive in the upper mesopelagic layer because AOU changed more during the intensifying stage than during the mature stage (Fig. 4e). This may imply enhanced POC consumption by microbial activity during the intensifying stage. The POC inventory change in the water column is the combined result of the POC flux supplied from the top and the POC consumption in the water column. It is thus very likely that the POC export flux was higher during the intensifying stage than during the mature stage, given that both the rate of change of POC and the average AOU were larger during the intensifying stage than during the mature stage.

The enhanced net POC flux during the eddy’s intensifying stage was then calculated using Eq. (5). Note that this flux should be smaller than the actual POC export flux, as POC consumption also increased during the intensifying stage compared with the mature stage (presented as a positive net rate of change of AOU) (Fig. 4e). An enhanced net POC flux of 1.68 ± 0.3 mmol C m−2 d−1 at ZEu was obtained, which was comparable to the estimates of POC export flux in the NPSG by sediment traps (1.92 mmol C m−2 d−1 by Grabowski et al.50 and 2.5 ± 0.7 mmol C m−2 d−1 by Zhou et al.31) and smaller than the estimates of POC export flux in the subpolar northwest Pacific Ocean using the radioactive technique (3.25 and 11.08 mmol C m−2 d−1 by Buesseler and Boyd51; Table S4). For eddies, significant POC export is not sustained throughout their lifespan and is often associated with the physical dynamics of eddies42,52. Observations have shown that intensifying eddies exhibit a large biological response, while eddies in the mature stage do not show a significant biological response or high export flux29,52. We assumed that the magnitude of the export flux during the eddy’s mature stage was low, so the enhanced net POC flux was considered as the approximation of the actual POC flux here. The enhanced POC flux may underestimate the actual POC flux during the eddy’s intensifying stage as F_EI(z) was a flux anomaly relative to the eddy’s mature stage. Because the Martin curve has long been used as the standard for quantifying POC attenuation across the global ocean, F_EI(z) values at different depths in the mesopelagic layer were fitted to the Martin curve (Eq. (8)) to estimate the attenuation coefficient b, yielding a value of 1.14 ± 0.24, which was similar to those estimated in subtropical gyres and higher than those estimated at high latitudes10,39,50,51 (Fig. 4g and Table S4).

POC flux by an intensifying submesoscale front
The sea surface temperature (SST) distribution revealed structures of a submesoscale thermal front with an SST gradient magnitude (GM) of ~0.2 °C km−1 outside of CE1 from 21 April to 3 May 2019 (Fig. S6a–d). During this period, float 2902753 drifted along the warm (upwelling) side of the front (Fig. S6). This was further supported by a Lagrangian particle tracking experiment, which suggested that the float drifted in a quasi-Lagrangian manner along one side of the front (Text S3). The front exhibited a higher temperature in the upper 300 m and lower salinity in the upper 150 m compared to the CE1 core, indicating that similar water masses were sampled in the frontal region. The T-S diagram demonstrated coherent physical characteristics from 21 April to 3 May 2019 (Fig. S7). All these results suggested that the float sampled similar water masses along the warm side of the front.

The float presented a small Richardson number Ri (Ri≈2) in the frontal region, indicating ageostrophic motions at play to a depth of ~250 m (Fig. S8b). The ageostrophic motions at the front can also be indicated by the increased finite-size Lyapunov exponent (FSLE) distributions at the front (Fig. S8c). We defined different stages of the front by examining changes of GM at the float locations. From 21 April to 27 April, the GM was elevated and larger than the background value, indicating that the float was sampling the front’s intensifying stage. From 28 April to 3 May, the GM decreased to the background value, indicative of the front’s decaying stage (Fig. S6e). In addition, the Ri between the MLD and 250 m depth was smaller during the intensifying stage than during the decaying stage (Fig. S8b). Consistent with the change of Ri, the magnitude of the lateral buoyancy frequency (M2) increased during the intensifying stage and decreased during the decaying stage (see the M2 envelope in Fig. S8c). During the intensifying stage, submesoscale dynamics were prone to generating secondary circulations across the front, which in turn changed the temperature and salinity distributions along the front. Due to the heterogeneous evolution and distribution of the front over time, M2 increased in magnitude along the front. The temporal changes in Ri and M2 suggested that submesoscale motions were more active during the intensifying stage than during the decaying stage. During the intensifying stage, the POC inventory in the euphotic zone was elevated (Fig. S9b). Moreover, large particles were detected by spikes of backscattering coefficients in the mesopelagic layer8 (Fig. S9c).

Given the two distinct periods sampled by the float, the rate of change of integrated POC during the intensifying (denoted as E_FI(z)) and decaying (denoted as E_FD(z)) stages of the front were calculated (Fig. 4b, d, f, h). The distribution of E_FD(z) was similar to that of E_EM(z), which decreased with depth (Fig. 4b, d). Following the same method applied to the eddy, the enhanced net POC flux induced by front intensification (denoted as F_FI(z)) was estimated by Eq. (6). In contrast to the eddy, the net rate of change of AOU was very small in the mesopelagic layer (Fig. 4f). The small net rate of change of AOU implies relatively stable POC consumption rates during the intensifying and decaying stages. The enhanced net POC flux (F_FI(z)) was thus mostly contributed by the increased POC export flux during the front intensifying stage (Fig. 4h). The increased POC export flux at the base of the euphotic zone was then approximately estimated as 2.11 ± 0.4 mmol C m−2 d−1, higher than that in the eddy’s intensifying stage. Similar results have been reported in the NPSG, which showed a higher POC flux at a submesoscale front than in a cyclonic eddy nearby (2.2 mmol C m−2 d−1 versus 1.2 mmol C m−2 d−1 in Guidi et al.41). In addition, an attenuation coefficient b of 0.56 ± 0.15 was estimated by fitting F_FI(z) to Eq. (8), which was smaller than that for the intensifying cyclonic eddy, implying deeper transfer of POC in the frontal region.
paper_content.methods:
BGC-Argo measurement and calibration
Data were collected by sensors equipped on the BGC-Argo floats from depths between ~900 m and the surface. The floats profiled twice a day. The floats sampled the first 30 m at a 0.2 m resolution, between 30–400 m at a 1 m resolution and below 400 m at a 5 m resolution. All profile data were interpolated at a 5 m resolution. Before deployment, the dark currents of the chlorophyll fluorometer and backscattering sensor were corrected (reassigned) based on the dark-current measurements, by masking the optical windows with black tape. The dark-corrected Chl and bbp profiles were smoothed using a 5-point moving median filter to minimize high frequency noise44. The spike of bbp(700), a qualitative proxy index for large particles, was calculated as the difference between the raw and smoothed bbp(700)8. The nitrate distributions from the BGC-Argo floats were calibrated using ship-based nitrate measurements taken along the BGC-Argo trajectories (Text S5 and Fig. S13). The ship-based POC concentrations were also measured during float deployment. Then, a localized statistical relationship between the bbp(700) values measured by the BGC-Argo floats and the ship-based collection of POC concentrations was derived (Text S5, Fig. S14; a total of 32 data points, R2=0.39, p<0.01):

POC (mmol C m−3) = 2083.17 * bbp(700) + 0.06 (1)

The mixed layer depth (MLD) was computed as the depth where the potential density was different from the sea surface density by 0.03 σθ following Jing et al.59. The ZEu was calculated as the depth where PAR was 1% of its surface value60. The AOU was calculated as the difference between the saturated and observed DO:

AOU = DOsat − DO (2)

where DOsat is the saturated DO computed using the measured temperature and salinity. To identify subsurface features resulting from subduction pumps, spiciness that describes thermohaline perturbations not included in potential density was estimated using the BGC-Argo-derived temperature and salinity data. As suggested by Omand et al.19, subsurface water masses originating from the euphotic zone were identified as subsurface anomalies in vertical POC and spiciness distributions.

Other data
Ship-based nitrate and POC measurements were collected at 10 stations near the BGC-Argo trajectories for nitrate calibration and POC calculations (Text S5 and Table S5). Nitrate was measured onboard using a Four-channel Continuous Flow Technicon AA3 Auto-Analyzer (Bran-Lube, GmbH). The POC data were determined using an Elemental vario EL cube CHNS Analyzer, of which the uncertainty was <10%42.

Daily SLA and sea surface Chl were obtained from the Copernicus Marine Environment Monitoring Service (CMEMS) and the Ocean Color Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI) project, respectively. The dataset from the Mesoscale Eddy Trajectory Atlas was identified and tracked using the methods provided by Pegliasco et al.12 and obtained from the Archiving, Validation, and Interpretation of Satellite Oceanographic Data (AVISO) service. Satellite-derived SST data at a resolution of ~4.5 km (available from the CMEMS) were used to determine the SST gradients of the oceanic fronts.

The rate of change of integrated POC
Since the float drifted along the front or in a relatively fixed position of CE2, we expected that the float sampled similar water masses over time. The POC concentrations derived from the float estimations were integrated from the base of the mesopelagic layer (900 m) to an upper mesopelagic depth z:

P(z) = ∫900m^z POC * dz (3)

where P(z) is the integrated POC, z=[ZEu, 200 m, 300 m, 400 m, 500 m]. The rate of change of integrated POC (denoted as E(z)) was thus considered as the net rate at which POC accumulated between depth z and the base of the mesopelagic layer:

E(z) = ∂P(z)/∂t (4)

where E(z) can be interpreted as the balance between the POC flux supply from depth z and the POC consumption between depth z and the base of the mesopelagic layer, given that the POC flux at the base of the mesopelagic layer is generally negligible10,46. The E(z) was calculated using a linear least squared method (slope of the regression line). Because the balance between supply and consumption is the driver of E(z) changes, we estimated E(z) during the intensifying and mature (decaying) stages of the eddy (front). The E(z) during the intensifying and mature stages of the eddy were denoted as E_EI(z) and E_EM(z), respectively, and those during the intensifying and decaying stages of the front were denoted as E_FI(z) and E_FD(z), respectively. The uncertainty of the linear least squared estimations was shown in Table S6. The enhanced net POC fluxes during the intensifying stages of the eddy (denoted as F_EI(z)) and the front (denoted as F_FI(z)) were calculated as:

F_EI(z) = E_EI(z) − E_EM(z) (5)

F_FI(z) = E_FI(z) − E_FD(z) (6)

A Lagrangian particle tracking experiment was conducted to test whether the float drifted along the front (Text S3). To further verify that the float sampled similar water masses, the physical characteristics along the front were analyzed (Fig. S7).

The AOU multiplied by the Redfield ratios represents the heterotrophic respiration of the total organic carbon (TOC), 50–90% of which is dissolved organic carbon48,61,62. Because the ratio of the POC to TOC and the Redfield ratios in the study region were not measured, we did not use the AOU to reconstruct the remineralized POC and only used the change of AOU over time to demonstrate possible changes in remineralization between different stages. The average AOU from the base of the mesopelagic layer (900 m) to an upper mesopelagic depth z was calculated as

average AOU = 1/(900m − z) * ∫900m^z AOU * dz (7)

where z=[ZEu, 200 m, 300 m, 400 m, 500 m]. The net rate of change of AOU defined as the difference of the temporal rate of AOU between the intensifying and mature (decaying) stages of the eddy (front) was thus estimated using the averaged AOU.

POC flux attenuation
The attenuation of POC flux with depth is quantified by a Martin curve63:

F(z) = F(ZEu) * (z/ZEu)^−b (8)

where F(z) is the POC flux at depth z, normalized to flux F(ZEu) at euphotic depth ZEu, and b is the attenuation coefficient.

The SST gradient
We use the SST gradient to indicate the strength of front. The SST gradient magnitude (GM) is calculated following Belkin and O’Reilly64:

GM = √(Gx^2 + Gy^2) (9)

where Gx and Gy are the zonal and meridional SST gradients that can be quantified as:

Gx = 1/dx * [1 0 −1; 6 0 −6; 1 0 −1] * SST (10)

Gy = 1/dy * [1 6 1; 0 0 0; −1 −6 −1] * SST (11)

where dx, dy and * are the zonal and meridional distances between successive pixels within the SST data and the convolution sign, respectively. Using satellite-derived SST data, the GM at the front where the BGC-Argo passed through (Fig. S6c–e) and at the locations of the sampling site for in-situ POC flux measurements (Fig. 5) were calculated. To extrapolate the relationship between the b value and GM for the NPSG, the spatial distributions of GM during 2003–2019 were also calculated (Text S6).

The FSLE field
We use the finite-size Lyapunov exponent (FSLE) to illustrate the frontal region encountered by the BGC-Argo. Daily FSLEs with a spatial resolution of 0.04° were obtained from AVISO. The FSLE is defined as the inverse time of separation of two particles from their initial distance δ0 to final distance δf65. The particles were advected by altimetry velocities and their trajectories were computed by backward-time integration of the altimetry velocities. The FSLE has been suggested to be particularly suited to diagnose filamentary processes generated by mesoscale horizontal shear and strain deformation65. Large backward FSLE values represent regions of strong submesoscale transport66. As such, the FSLE has been employed to delineate submesoscale structures32,66. The FSLE time series was extracted along the path of float 2902753 to capture the strain field and was then compared to the lateral buoyancy frequency (M2) sampled by the float.

The manuscript by Wang et al., used two high-frequency sampling BGC-Argo deployed in the western Pacific to invesfigate the impact of the eddies on the POC export. The authors reported enhanced POC export in the regions affected by intensifying submesoscale fronts and further meta-analysis of a global compiled dataset revealed a prevailing relafionship between transfer efficiency and the strength of submesoscale front (indicafive of surface temperature gradient). Finally, the authors upscaled the contribufion of eddies to the carbon export in the enfire northern subtropical Pacific gyre by synthesizing the frequency of eddy occurrence.
However, I find several noteworthy loopholes in the BGC-Argo data analysis, specially related to the observed AOU rate, and its discrepancy with the POC rate. See my explicit comments below:
1) Unexpected, negafive change of AOU and the discrepancy between AOU and POC rate:
Figure 3 shows the author derived negafive values for the fime rate of AOU in many cases, the implicafion being that twilight zone oxygen increases over fime. This tendency is somewhat surprising to me, as we generally expect a declining trend of oxygen over fime below the euphofic zone resulfing from biological respirafion, regardless of the relafive change in upper POC flux.
Furthermore, the reported magnitude of AOU rate appears to be unrealisfically high. The depth-integrated AOU rates between 150m (or 170m) and 900m fall within the range of 250-500 mmol m-2 d-1, equivalent to 90-180 mmol m-2 yr-1. For comparison, the global range of upper carbon export is only typically 1-4 mol C m-2 yr-1. These extremely high AOU rates also are sharply analogous relafive to export flux solved from POC inventory, which falls within the range of 1-2 mmol C m-2 d-1.
I suspect there are two possible reasons for the discrepancies. It is well known that the evolufion of eddy typically results in a significant displacement of water masses. Thereby, observed AOU and POC change rates along the isobars may reflect a confounding result of both biological and physical processes. Therefore, to befter isolate the biologically-induced tracer change that the authors are interested in, it would be more appropriate to quanfify the fime rate change of AOU (and POC as well) along with the isopycncal surfaces.
The second possible reason is the float didn’t exactly track the same water mass and may gradually move towards a region featured with a higher pre-formed oxygen concentrafion. Responses to Reviewers
We thank the four reviewers for their constructive comments and suggestions, which
we believe have considerably improved our manuscript now entitled ‘Efficient
biological carbon export to the mesopelagic ocean induced by submesoscale fronts’.
We have responded point-by-point to the reviewers’ questions and comments below.
All page/line/reference/figure numbers refer to the tracked manuscript. Reviewers’
comments are in regular text, our responses are in blue and new text from the
manuscript is in blue italics.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This study presents an observation-based analysis of the relationship between
particulate organic carbon (POC) and eddy and frontal dynamics. The authors have
leveraged observations from floats with the objective to bring new insights into carbon
export dynamics at fine scale. This is a valuable effort; yet there are major issues that
need to be addressed before it can be published. The main concerns fall in 4 categories:
I. Gaps in context and references to prior work in introduction and discussion of the
results, specifically the potential impact of frontal subduction (comment #1)
II. Missing or weak justification of the hypotheses used to interpret the data that account
for the compounding effects of spatial and temporal variability, specifically the
justification to use a “mostly spatial” or a “mostly temporal” framework depending on
the eddy/front considered (comments #2-5)
III. Shortcomings with the conclusions and generalizations of the results that link fronts
to POC export and attenuation coefficient b, which is the main point of the paper
(comments # 6-10).
IV. Imprecisions on the approach that need clarification, issues with text and figures.
(comments #11-28).
Detailed comments and suggestions on how to address them are provided below. The
two reviewers that contributed to this review believe the authors can improve the
justification of their approach, as well as the interpretation and generalization so the
manuscript can be acceptable for publication.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive suggestions. We
find that the paper is significantly strengthened by addressing the four issues you are
concerned with. We have responded to these questions and comments point-by-point
below.
1. Gaps in context and references. The sentence of L71 is not true: “In this study, for
the first time, we show the capability of using BGC-Argo floats equipped with optical
sensors to estimate the carbon export flux and associated vertical attenuation in
response to submesoscale fronts”
The paper is lacking key references, in particular prior studies identifying and
quantifying the role of subduction by fronts, including with BGC-Argo floats. The
manuscript leads us to believe that there were no attempts to quantify this subduction
pump before. Yet observation based (using float AOU, spiciness) and high resolution
modeling papers have been published on this topic (see list of reference below). They
need to be included to provide the adequate context in the introduction but also in the
discussion. Note that the process of export by subduction along fronts explained in this
study can be called differently in the literature: eddy pump, eddy subduction pump etc.
Although the term “eddy pump” was often used, it does not usually refer to “Ekman
pumping” in eddies but the subduction by fast velocities associated with meso and
submesoscale fronts, similarly to what is considered in this manuscript.
Sentences that critically need these references include L56-67 (almost all sentences in
this paragraph are missing critical references), L71 which needs to integrate these prior
work. In discussion, please consider how the impact of subduction would influence
your results and discuss considering these prior works.
Review about export pumps including the physical injection pump or eddy pump:
Boyd, P.W., Claustre, H., Levy, M., Siegel, D.A., Weber, T., 2019. Multi-faceted particle
pumps drive carbon sequestration in the ocean. Nature 568, 327.
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1098-2
Papers estimating the role the “eddy subduction pump” using BGC-Argo, cruises and
models:
Erickson, Z.K., Thompson, A.F., 2018. The Seasonality of Physically Driven Export at
Submesoscales in the Northeast Atlantic Ocean. Global Biogeochemical Cycles 32.
https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GB005927
Lacour, L., Llort, J., Briggs, N., Strutton, P.G., Boyd, P.W., 2023. Seasonality of
downward carbon export in the Pacific Southern Ocean revealed by multi-year robotic
observations. Nat Commun 14, 1278. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-36954-7
Llort, J., Langlais C., Matear R., Moreau S., Lenton A., Strutton Peter G., 2018.
Evaluating Southern Ocean Carbon Eddy‐Pump From Biogeochemical‐Argo Floats.
Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans 123, 971–984.
https://doi.org/10.1002/2017JC012861
McGillicuddy, D.J., Resplandy, L., Lévy, M., 2019. Estimating particle export flux from
satellite observations: Challenges associated with spatial and temporal decoupling of
production and export. Journal of Marine Research 77, 247–258.
https://doi.org/10.1357/002224019828474331
Omand, M.M., D’Asaro, E.A., Lee, C.M., Perry, M.J., Briggs, N., Cetinić, I.,
Mahadevan, A., 2015. Eddy-driven subduction exports particulate organic carbon from
the spring bloom. Science 348, 222–225. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1260062
Resplandy, L., Lévy, M., McGillicuddy Jr., D.J., 2019. Effects of Eddy-Driven
Subduction on Ocean Biological Carbon Pump. Global Biogeochemical Cycles 33,
1071–1084. https://doi.org/10.1029/2018GB006125
Stukel, M.R., Song, H., Goericke, R., Miller, A.J., 2017. The role of subduction and
gravitational sinking in particle export, carbon sequestration, and the remineralization
length scale in the California Current Ecosystem: Subduction and sinking particle
export in the CCE. Limnology and Oceanography 63, 363–383.
https://doi.org/10.1002/lno.10636
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that prior works on subduction
by fronts should be included in the introduction, and its impacts on our results should
be discussed, as subduction by fronts is one of the most important dynamics by which
submesoscale processes affect local POC distributions. We deleted that inaccurate
statement in this revision. The changes in the introduction and discussion sections are
summarized below:
1. Changes in the introduction section
To provide a more adequate context in the introduction that the submesoscale process
affects local POC export, we first added one sentence in Lines 57-60 to mention the
eddy-subduction pump:
‘The vertical motions can inject high POC produced in the euphotic zone into the
mesopelagic layer (referred to as eddy subduction pumps)17,19,22,24, resulting in long-
term carbon sequestration17,19,20,23.’
Second, prior works that attempted to identify and quantify eddy subduction pumps
have been acknowledged in Lines 68-71:
‘Prior studies have captured anomalous features of elevated POC at depth, which are
interpreted as evidence of eddy subduction pump19,22,23. Despite their potential
importance in shaping POC export, direct observations of the downward POC flux and
its attenuation in response to submesoscale fronts are scarce17,19-21,23,41.’
and Lines 76-81 :
‘Observational and high-resolution modeling studies have suggested that the eddy
subduction pump contributes ~19% to 50% to the total export of POC. In contrast,
Resplandy et al. (2019) explored the integrated effects of eddy subduction hot spots on
the biological carbon pump and found that they contribute less than 5% to carbon
export due to the strong compensation between upward and downward fluxes.’
Additionally, key references have been added in Lines 71 (Omand et al., 2015; Llort et
al., 2018; Erickson et al., 2018; Lacour et al., 2023; Boyd et al., 2019) and Line 86
(Llort et al., 2018; Lacour et al., 2023).
Finally, we acknowledge that Llort et al. (2018) was the first to quantify the carbon
export flux associated with submesoscale fronts by using BGC-Argo. Previous studies
that quantified the carbon export flux at submesoscale using BGC-Argo have also been
cited in this revision. In comparison, however, these previous studies didn’t consider
the vertical attenuation of the carbon flux at submesoscale fronts, which is the main
contribution of our study. To integrate the previous efforts and clarify the novelty of
our results, we have rephrased the sentence as shown below (Lines 91-96):
‘The BGC-Argo has been used to identify elevated POC in the mesopelagic layer and
estimate the carbon flux associated with submesoscale features20,23. In this study, we
further show the capability of using BGC-Argo floats to estimate the transfer efficiency
of carbon export in response to submesoscale fronts.’
2. Discussion on the impacts of subduction on POC export
We agree with comments #8 and #9 that the impacts of subduction by front should be
taken into account to interpret our results. More discussion has been added in this
revision.
As you mentioned in comment #9, the high POC at a depth of 200 m at the edge of CE
1 could be due to subduction of POC from the productive layer by the front. After a
detailed examination, we agree with this comment and have added additional text
(Lines 376-382) to discuss this point. Please see our response to this comment #9.
On the other hand, we found that the influence depth of eddy subduction may not be
deep enough to affect the lower mesopelagic layer. The elevated POC concentration
and flux were only present at depths between Z and ~250 m. We tested different ways
Eu
to fit the POC flux attenuation coefficient (b) with and without considering the POC
flux in the subduction layer (Z ~250 m). The b value was about 0.65 excluding the
Eu
POC flux in the eddy subduction layer, which was higher than that considering the
subduction layer (b=0.56), but was still lower than those estimated in eddies and normal
conditions. This suggests that submesoscale dynamics affect POC export flux not only
through physical subduction but also through modulating particle properties (e.g., size,
sinking speed and composition). We have added a paragraph (Lines 373-393) to fully
discuss the impact of eddy subduction on our results. Please find our detailed response
to comment #8.
References:
Boyd, P.W., Claustre, H., Levy, M., Siegel, D.A., Weber, T., 2019. Multi-faceted particle
pumps drive carbon sequestration in the ocean. Nature 568, 327–335 (2019).
Resplandy, L., Lévy, M. & Mcgillicuddy, D. J. Effects of eddy-driven subduction on
ocean biological carbon pump. Glob. Biogeochem. Cycles 33, 1071–1084 (2019).
Omand, M. M. et al. Eddy-driven subduction exports particulate organic carbon from
the spring bloom. Science 348, 222–225 (2015).
Lacour, L., Llort, J., Briggs, N. et al. Seasonality of downward carbon export in the
Pacific Southern Ocean revealed by multi-year robotic observations. Nat. Commun. 14,
1278 (2023).
Erickson, Z. K. & Thompson, A. F. The seasonality of physically driven export at
submesoscales in the Northeast Atlantic Ocean. Global Biogeochem. Cycles 32, 1144–
1162 (2018).
Stukel, M. R., Song, H., Goericke, R. & Miller, A. J. The role of subduction and
gravitational sinking in particle export, carbon sequestration, and the remineralization
length scale in the California Current Ecosystem. Limnol. Oceanogr. 63, 363–383
(2018).
Llort, J. et al. Evaluating Southern Ocean carbon eddy-pump from biogeochemical-
argo floats. J. Geophys. Res. Ocean. 123, 971–984 (2018).
McGillicuddy, D. J. et al. Estimating particle export flux from satellite observations:
Challenges associated with spatial and temporal decoupling of production and export.
J. Mar. Res. 77, 247–258 (2019).
Lévy, M. et al. The Impact of Fine-Scale Currents on Biogeochemical Cycles in a
Changing Ocean. Annu. Rev. Mar. Sci. 16,1 (2024).
2. Missing justification of the hypotheses, specifically the justification to use a “mostly
spatial” or a “mostly temporal” framework to interpret the float data.
The authors alternatively interpret the observed changes along the float trajectories as
“mostly spatial changes” (CE1 and ACE1, Figure 2), or “mostly temporal changes” i.e.
pseudo lagrangian (CE2 and front, Figure 3). The hypothesis of “mostly temporal” is
justified in the text for CE2 (L128 and 141). However, the justification to interpret as
“mostly spatial” the changes along CE1 and ACE1 is missing, and the hypothesis to
interpret as “mostly temporal” the changes attributed to frontal dynamics seems
inadequate (see details in comments 3 and 4 below). We encourage the authors to
explain clearly and early these different strategies to orient and prepare the reader.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. In this study, we performed different
analyses based on different sampling scenarios of the floats to delineate temporal and
spatial variabilities of the measured variable. For the hypothesis of ‘most spatial
changes’ in eddies (CE1 and ACE1), we first showed a radial increase of the relative
distance between the float and the eddy center with time. Then, we demonstrated that
the change of surface Chl measured by the floats was consistent with the radial variation
of remote-sensed surface Chl from the eddy core to the eddy edge. In addition, with
remote sensing data, we can track the temporal evolution of Chl in eddies, and this
temporal pattern was completely different from the change of float-measured surface
Chl. Therefore, for this sampling period, we think the float-measured variability of POC
can be used to represent the spatial variability of POC from the eddy core to the eddy
edge.
For the hypothesis of ‘most temporal changes’ along a submesoscale front, we added
more analysis about the float-measured characteristics of the water masses. We also
conducted a numerical particle tracking experiment. These new results all suggest that
the float continuously drifted along the warm side of the front on which homogeneous
water masses were sampled. During this period, the front experienced intensifying and
decaying stages, while the float was still sampling along its warm side. As such, the
float observations at the front can be interpreted as a temporal signal due to the stage
change of the front.
Following the suggestions, we now justify these two hypotheses early in Sections 2.1
and 2.3, respectively. Please see more details in our following responses to comments
#3 and #4.
3. The authors need to demonstrate why it is justified to ignore temporal variations
when analyzing CE1 and ACE1. Figure 2 interprets all POC data as spatial changes
(using radial structure of the eddies CE1 and ACE1). The approach is attractive, but the
text and figures should clearly show that this is a valid hypothesis. Specifically, how
much of the signal that is interpreted as spatial variability across the eddy is in fact
introduced by the temporal evolution along the trajectory of the float? At least, the
authors could indicate the day of sampling for each data point on Figure 2? [Colors
could indicate the day of sampling while symbols could indicate the depth]. This would
allow the reader to see how much of the variations attributed to the spatial structure of
the eddy could be introduced by temporal changes.
Response: Thank you for the constructive comment. For CE 1 and ACE 1, we
interpreted the measured variability of POC as the radial structures of eddies based on
the following considerations:
Firstly, there was an increasing relative distance between the float and the eddy center
with time. The location of the float changed from inside the eddy to outside the eddy,
with a relative distance of r/R between 0.4~2.0 for CE 1 and 0.23~1.2 for ACE 1.
Secondly, the spatial distribution of Chl in eddies was derived by compositing the
remote-sensed sea surface Chl over the float sampling period. This satellite-derived Chl
was then interpolated onto the relative locations of the float in eddies to compare with
that measured by the float. In CE 1, both the satellite- and float-derived Chl decreased
and then increased in the radial direction, reaching a peak at r/R=1~1.5 (Fig. S2). In
ACE 1, both the satellite- and float-derived Chl showed a double peak pattern along the
radial direction (Fig. S2a). The correlations between the satellite- and float-derived Chl
were 0.39 (p=0.01) and 0.43 (p=0.09) for CE1 and ACE 1, respectively. The relatively
consistent changing patterns of Chl between the float and remote sensing data suggest
that the float captured the spatial variability of the eddies in the radial direction.
Lastly, it is likely that the temporal signal was also included in the float data as it
exhibited larger 95% confidence intervals than those derived from satellite observations
(Fig. S2a). With remote sensing data, we can track the temporal evolution of the Chl in
eddies, and this temporal pattern was completely different from the change of float-
measured surface Chl (Fig. S2b). The correlations between the satellite- and float-
derived Chl over time were -0.18 (p=0.24) and -0.05 (p=0.82) for CE1 and ACE 1,
respectively, suggesting that the variability explained by the temporal evolution of Chl
of eddies was much small. Therefore, for this sampling period, we think the float-
measured variability of variables can be used to represent the spatial variability of
eddies.
To clarify this point, we added the following sentences in Lines 143-154 and Fig. S2
before we presented the radial POC distributions in the text:
‘The floats may capture the spatial variability of tracers for CE 1 and ACE 1 as the
location of the floats changed from inside the eddies to outside the eddies. The satellite-
derived sea surface Chl was averaged over the float sampling period and then
interpolated onto the relative locations of the float in eddies to compare with that
measured by the float. The float-measured Chl was in good agreement with that derived
from satellites in the radial direction (Fig. S2a), with correlations of 0.39 (p=0.01) for
CE1 and 0.43 (p=0.09) for ACE 1. In contrast, the temporal evolution of satellite-
derived Chl averaged inside eddies was completely different from that of float-
measured Chl (Fig. S2b), indicated by low correlations (R= -0.18 (p=0.24) for CE 1
and R=-0.05 (p=0.82) for ACE 1). Therefore, the float-measured tracers during this
period can be used to represent the spatial variability of the eddies along the radial
direction.’
Another thing worth mentioning is that the high POC distribution at the edge of CE 1
was due to subduction by the front (please see our reply to comment #9). This further
strengthens the point that the distributions of POC captured by the float reflect the
spatial variability of the eddy. We have added the following sentence in Lines 169-170
to emphasize this point:
‘This further supports that the radial distributions of POC measured by the float reflect
the spatial variability of the eddy.’
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, colors have been indicated in Fig. 2. For CE 1, as
the float moved almost monotonically from the eddy core to the edge with time, it is
still not easy to tell the influence of the temporal signal from this figure. Figure R1
shows the variations of the strength of the eddies. It is clear that although CE 1 was
strengthened in early May while the float was at r/R=~1.3, the float-measured POC at
SCM layer was still lower than that measured at the eddy core (Fig. 3), implying
dominant variability caused by space instead of time.
Figure S2. Comparison of sea surface Chl between satellite and BGC-Argo
observations in both spatial and temporal variability. a Radial distribution of sea surface
Chl at the float locations derived from both the BGC-Argo and satellite observations.
The BGC-Argo results are directly obtained from the surface Chl measured by the float.
The satellite-derived Chl values are calculated by averaging the Chl from OC-CCI over
the float sampling period and then interpolating to the relative locations of the float in
eddies. Because the eddies propagated over time, the location of the float in the eddies
was constructed by calculating the azimuthal and radial positions of the float relative to
the eddy center. b Satellite-derived Chl averaged inside eddies and sea surface Chl
derived from BGC-Argo observations. The BGC-Argo results are directly obtained
from the surface Chl measured by the float. The satellite-derived Chl values are
calculated by averaging the satellite-derived Chl values inside the eddies at the time
when the float was at the position of r/R.
Figure 3. POC distributions at different depths within a CE 1 and b ACE 1.
Figure R1. Evolution of SLA averaged inside eddies.The SLA values are calculated by
averaging the SLA inside the eddies at the time when the float was at the position of
r/R.
4. The hypothesis of “mostly temporal” is highly disputable for the front. It is ok for
eddy CE2 because the float seems to stay stuck close to the center of the eddy, and most
changes can be interpreted as temporal changes. In the case of the front, however, the
float seems to be sampling different parts of the front. The associated changes in SLA,
POC, AOU etc. are therefore likely to come from spatial variations across the front and
not temporal variations. The authors could demonstrate that it is indeed temporal,
however it is unlikely to be successful and convincing given the complexity of the
dynamics in the frontal structure. This shortcoming has major implications for the result
interpretation and the conclusions of the paper as the authors interpret these changes as
temporal changes while they are likely spatial changes. This section of the results and
associated conclusions needs to be revised.
Response: Thank you for the insightful comment. According to the frontogenesis
theory, when the front is enhanced, it will generate downwelling on the cold side of the
front and upwelling on the warm side of the front. The hypothesis of ‘mostly temporal’
is that the float drifted along one side of the front so that relatively homogeneous water
masses over time were sampled. During this period, the front experienced intensifying and
decaying stages, while the float was still sampling along its one side. As such, the
float observations at the front can be interpreted as a temporal signal due to the stage
change of the front. We have provided more justifications in the revised text to interpret
this hypothesis.
By investigating the time series of FSLE along the float trajectory, we found that the
float traveled along the same filament with high FSLEs. This result, in combination
with the Chl, SST and SST gradient distributions (already shown), demonstrated that
the float continuously traveled along the warm side of a front during that period.
To further support that the float drifted along one front, a numerical particle tracking
experiment was conducted at the frontal region using the TRACMASS code. The
particle was released at the same location as the float on 21 April 2019 and it was moved
purely by advection using the surface geostrophic current derived from AVISO data.
The numerical tracking results showed that the float mainly followed the path of the
particle (Fig. S14), suggesting that the float moved in a quasi-Lagrangian manner and
sampled a similar water mass during the analysis period (supplementary information
Text S3).
The homogeneous water masses sampled on one side of the front can be supported by
the transect of temperature and salinity anomalies (Fig. S6). The temperature was
higher in the upper 300 m and the salinity was lower in the upper 150 m depth compared
to the CE 1 core. In addition, the T-S diagram presents a coherent physical characteristic
from 21 April to 3 May 2019, suggesting that the float was moving along the front but
not across the front.
Overall, these results support the use of the float data as a time series on the warm side
of the front during the analysis period.
We have clarified this point in the text in Lines 247-250:
‘This is further supported by a Lagrangian particle tracking experiment, which
suggests that the float drifted in a quasi-Lagrangian manner and sampled a similar
water mass along one side of the front (Text S3).’
, and Lines 250-255:
‘The front exhibited a higher temperature in the upper 300 m and lower salinity in lower salinity in the
upper 150 m depth compared to the CE 1 core (Fig. S6), suggesting homogeneous water
masses sampled at the frontal region. The T-S diagram demonstrates a coherent
physical characteristic from 21 April to 3 May 2019 (Fig. S6). All these results suggest
that the float sampled homogeneous water masses along the warm side of the front.’
Text S3. Lagrangian particle tracking experiment on the front
To investigate whether the float drifted along the front, a numerical particle tracking
experiment was conducted using the TRACMASS Lagrangian trajectory code (Döös,
1995; Blanke & Raynaud, 1997). The particle was released at the same location as the
float on 21 April 2019 and transported purely by surface current. Here, we run the code
with the current velocity derived from AVISO. The Lagrangian particle trajectory
derived from the particle tracking model demonstrated that the virtual particle starting
at the location of the float moved along the front (Fig S14). The float moved slower
than the particle but mainly followed its path, suggesting that the float drifted in a
quasi-Lagrangian manner during the analysis period. The difference in moving velocity
is that the particle was only transported by surface current, whereas the motion of the
float was driven by both the surface and deep currents.
Figure S14. Trajectories of the BGC-Argo and the virtual particle over the period when
the float was on the front (21 April - 3 May 2019). The particle was released at the same
position as the float on 21 April 2019 and transported by the surface current velocity
derived from AVISO. The particle trajectory was tracked using the TRACMASS code.
Color indicates the dates. Blue and red lines are the contour lines of the sea level
anomaly (SLA). Arrows represent the sea surface current velocity anomaly.
Figure S6. Physical characteristics of the float measurements. During 21 April - 3 May
2019, the float was on one side of the front. Time series of a temperature, b salinity, c
temperature anomaly and d salinity anomaly measured by float 2902753 from 1 April
to 3 May 2019. The black, red and cyan lines indicate the mixed layer depth (MLD),
the depth of subsurface chlorophyll maximum (Z ) and the euphotic zone (Z ),
SCM Eu
respectively. The white lines are the isopycnals of 23, 24 and 25 kg m-3. The temperature
and salinity anomalies were defined as the instantaneous values after subtracting the
full time mean. e Temperature-salinity diagram with data points from float 2902753
from 1 April to 3 May 2019. The color indicates the sampling date.
5. The sampling context should be better presented. In Figure 1, eddies and float
trajectories appear completely disconnected. This is likely because the black lines show
the center of the eddy and not their span. Could you indicate the radius of the eddies
around the trajectories so we can see that they were indeed in the eddies? Also we
encourage the authors to include a figure similar to Figure S4a to show the float relative
to the eddy/front. Maybe choose snapshots that show the overlap with the front as a
function of time.
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. The gray lines indicating the eddy radius
have been overlapped in Fig. 1a to show the connection of the eddy centers and the
floats. Additionally, snapshots showing the locations of the floats relative to the eddies
and the front have been included in the new Figure 2.
Figure 2. The BGC-Argo and eddy trajectories. a The locations of (yellow dots) the
BGC-Argo float (WMO number 2902753) and (orange pentagrams) the center of
cyclonic eddy 1 (CE 1) during 1-20 April 2019. b The locations of (yellow dots) the
BGC-Argo float (WMO number 2902753) and (orange pentagrams) the center of
anticyclonic eddy 1 (ACE 1) during 12 July - 2 September 2019. c The locations of
(yellow dots) the BGC-Argo float (WMO number 2902756) and (orange pentagrams)

6. Generalization between front and carbon export. L214-222. “A strong correlation
between the b value and GM was found …. This statistical relationship implies that a
strong front is linked with high POC transfer efficiency to the mesopelagic layer, which
could be used as a parameterization to account for the impact of fronts on carbon export
in large-scale models, once the front intensity at the surface is known”. This conclusion
seems not backed up by the results. More complete models seem to show that b can
vary according to many other biophysical parameters, making this generalization highly
debatable (see for instance Ngyuen et al. 2022: Microbes contribute to setting the ocean
carbon flux by altering the fate of sinking particulates). This is one of the main points
of the paper; the caveats need to be discussed properly.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that a parametrization of the b
value as a function of the front intensity is inadequate since the efficiency of POC
transfer is modulated by complicated physical and biogeochemical processes. We have
rephrased the sentence as follows to be clearer:
‘This statistical relationship implies that a strong front is linked with high POC transfer
efficiency to the mesopelagic layer, which could be used to estimate the impact of fronts
on carbon export at the basin-scale oceans.’
We used this relationship to estimate the impacts of fronts on POC transfer efficiency.
The underlying mechanism is that submesoscale dynamics play a role through their
impact on the particle sinking velocity or particle lability. The following discussion has
been added to the manuscript (Lines 405-413):
‘The estimation suggests that submesoscale fronts are important in setting the spatial
and temporal variations in POC transfer efficiency. Previous carbon cycle studies have
suggested that the attenuation of the POC flux is determined by the rate of POC

processes include mixed layer pumping, bacterial colonization and consumption,
zooplankton migration, consumption, and fragmentation. However, there are no clear
data or previous studies showing why these processes could be particularly enhanced

processes may allow a better constraint in estimating POC transfer efficiency, but it
definitely requires future work to examine how submesoscale dynamics affect these

fragmentation by zooplankton8) were not explicitly included in the estimation.

estimated from sediment traps or radioactive techniques recorded in the literature.

theory, when the front is enhanced, it will generate downwelling on the cold side of the
front and upwelling on the warm side of the front. The hypothesis of ‘mostly temporal’
is that the float drifted along one side of the front so that relatively homogeneous water
masses over time were sampled. During this period, the front experienced intensifying and
decaying stages, while the float was still sampling along its one side. As such, the
float observations at the front can be interpreted as a temporal signal due to the stage
change of the front. We have provided more justifications in the revised text to interpret

By investigating the time series of FSLE along the float trajectory, we found that the
float traveled along the same filament with high FSLEs. This result, in combination

higher in the upper 300 m and the salinity was lower in the upper 150 m depth compared
to the CE 1 core. In addition, the T-S diagram presents a coherent physical characteristic
from 21 April to 3 May 2019, suggesting that the float was moving along the front but
not across the front.

of the front during the analysis period.

Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that a parametrization of the b
value as a function of the front intensity is inadequate since the efficiency of POC
transfer is modulated by complicated physical and biogeochemical processes. We have
rephrased the sentence as follows to be clearer:
‘This statistical relationship implies that a strong front is linked with high POC transfer
efficiency to the mesopelagic layer, which could be used to estimate the impact of fronts
on carbon export at the basin-scale oceans.’
We used this relationship to estimate the impacts of fronts on POC transfer efficiency.
The underlying mechanism is that submesoscale dynamics play a role through their
impact on the particle sinking velocity or particle lability. The following discussion has
been added to the manuscript (Lines 405-413):
‘The estimation suggests that submesoscale fronts are important in setting the spatial
and temporal variations in POC transfer efficiency. Previous carbon cycle studies have
suggested that the attenuation of the POC flux is determined by the rate of POC
production in the euphotic zone, the sinking velocity of particles, and the rate of POC
consumption in the mesopelagic layer5-10,38,39,49-54. Submesoscale dynamics may play a
role in POC flux transfer through eddy subduction that directly enhances the particle
sinking velocity or through its impacts on the plankton community structure in the
euphotic zone that generates particles with large sinking velocities and/or low
remineralization rates9,14-23,32.’
The caveat of the estimation conducted in this study is that we did not explicitly include
other physical and biogeochemical processes that affect POC flux attenuation. These
processes include mixed layer pumping, bacterial colonization and consumption,
zooplankton migration, consumption, and fragmentation. However, there are no clear

anomaly approaches the total POC flux, and can be compared with those directly
estimated from sediment traps or radioactive techniques recorded in the literature.

Review comment
The manuscript by Wang et al., used two high-frequency sampling BGC-Argo deployed
in the western Pacific to investigate the impact of the eddies on the POC export. The
authors reported enhanced POC export in the regions affected by intensifying
submesoscale fronts and further meta-analysis of a global compiled dataset revealed a
prevailing relationship between transfer efficiency and the strength of submesoscale
front (indicative of surface temperature gradient). Finally, the authors upscaled the
contribution of eddies to the carbon export in the entire northern subtropical Pacific
gyre by synthesizing the frequency of eddy occurrence.

Response: We thank the reviewer for providing helpful suggestions and pointing out
the discrepancy between the AOU and POC results. We have responded to these
questions and comments point-by-point below. We find that the paper is significantly
strengthened by addressing these issues.
1) Unexpected, negative change of AOU and the discrepancy between AOU and POC
rate:
Figure 3 shows the author derived negative values for the time rate of AOU in many
cases, the implication being that twilight zone oxygen increases over time. This
tendency is somewhat surprising to me, as we generally expect a declining trend of
oxygen over time below the euphotic zone resulting from biological respiration,
regardless of the relative change in upper POC flux.
Furthermore, the reported magnitude of AOU rate appears to be unrealistically high.
The depth-integrated AOU rates between 150m (or 170m) and 900m fall within the
range of 250-500 mmol m-2 d-1, equivalent to 90-180 mol m-2 yr-1. For comparison,
the global range of upper carbon export is only typically 1-4 mol C m-2 yr-1. These
extremely high AOU rates also are sharply analogous relative to export flux solved from
POC inventory, which falls within the range of 1-2 mmol C m-2 d-1.
I suspect there are two possible reasons for the discrepancies. It is well known that the
evolution of eddy typically results in a significant displacement of water masses.
Thereby, observed AOU and POC change rates along the isobars may reflect a
confounding result of both biological and physical processes. Therefore, to better
isolate the biologically-induced tracer change that the authors are interested in, it would
be more appropriate to quantify the time rate change of AOU (and POC as well) along
with the isopycncal surfaces.
The second possible reason is the float didn’t exactly track the same water mass and
may gradually move towards a region featured with a higher pre-formed oxygen
